records.title: Electric streetcars and urban traction
records.sourceNativeSummary: Electric traction converted central-station/motor capability into a dense urban transport system. Washington's electric cars appeared in 1888 and line mileage expanded rapidly; the useful artifact included track, overhead/conduit power, substations/operations and larger rolling stock, not the motor alone.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Horse/cable traction were real incumbents; electrification value depended on route density, power infrastructure and urban operating economics, so a motor success did not imply every transport route should electrify immediately.

sources.supports: 1888 Washington electrification and large urban line system

records.title: Factory electrification from line shafts toward unit drive
records.sourceNativeSummary: Electric motors gradually freed machine placement from long mechanical shafts/pulleys. The productivity benefit often required factory redesign around process flow rather than swapping one prime mover while leaving layout unchanged.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Existing line-shaft factories were functional and sunk-capital rich; electrical flexibility only paid when layout/control/process changes exploited it, so capability availability could precede productivity realization by years.

sources.supports: electric motors freeing machine placement and process-specific layout

records.title: Recorded sound: phonograph cylinders versus gramophone discs
records.sourceNativeSummary: Edison's 1877 phonograph made record-and-playback physically real; early tinfoil recordings were fragile and replay-limited. Wax cylinders and Berliner's flat disc/gramophone created different reproduction/storage/manufacturing worlds; disc mastering enabled scalable copying.
records.rivalOrBoundary: The first playback machine did not define the mass-recording industry. Cylinder and disc routes traded recording convenience, durability, storage and duplication, and an initially spectacular invention could pause for years before better media/business systems made it durable.

sources.supports: 1877 phonograph, fragile tinfoil and wax-cylinder return

records.title: Motion pictures: chronophotography, Kinetoscope and projected cinema
records.sourceNativeSummary: Muybridge/Marey decomposed motion into image sequences; Edison/Dickson developed a practical film camera and peephole Kinetoscope; projected systems then overtook single-viewer cabinets. The trajectory required film stock, camera transport, viewing/projection and exhibition economics.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Kinetoscope parlors were commercially real before projection displaced them. A locally successful representation/display architecture can lose when audience-scale economics change; that does not make its original performance false.

records.title: Audion triode: detector to amplification substrate
records.sourceNativeSummary: De Forest's 1906–07 three-element Audion began as a radio detector; by 1912 the grid-controlled tube was adapted as an amplifier and later oscillator. A component's productive identity changed as circuit use and vacuum/device understanding improved.
records.rivalOrBoundary: The early Audion was not born as a mature universal amplifier and performance was unstable. Later enormous option value should not be projected backward as proof that the original detector implementation was already a complete electronics platform.

sources.supports: 1906–07 detector, 1912 amplifier and later oscillator lineage

records.title: Global submarine-telegraph network operations after initial Atlantic success
records.sourceNativeSummary: After durable Atlantic service became possible, submarine cables expanded into a global network. The frontier shifted from proving one ocean cable to route redundancy, landing stations, repair ships, international ownership, message tariffs and geopolitical control of cable paths.
records.rivalOrBoundary: A working cable route could still be strategically fragile or monopolized; network value and resilience depended on alternate routes/repair capacity, not raw cable length. Wireless later became a rival complement rather than instantly eliminating cable.

sources.supports: Atlantic cable expedition/operations lineage and marine repair infrastructure
international telegraph coordination pressure preceding expanded network
later transition from telegraph network to radiotelegraph coordination

records.title: Good Roads movement as bicycle/automobile infrastructure complement
records.sourceNativeSummary: Most rural U.S. roads remained dirt/gravel while bicycles and automobiles increased demand for reliable intercity travel. The Good Roads movement built a political/information layer around paving, route mapping and national-road advocacy; bicycle organizations were early promoters before automobiles became dominant beneficiaries.
records.rivalOrBoundary: Vehicle improvement alone could not remove muddy/seasonal road constraints. Conversely, road investment had distributional/public-finance consequences and should not be counted as an intrinsic property of any one automobile technology.

sources.supports: bicycle origins, rural road pressure, 1911 National Highways Association and route maps
